issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: For a natural-disaster trauma, 'specific body parts associated with the event' is hard to reconcile clinically unless the disaster involved gruesome injury exposure, which is not supported elsewhere in the profile. The other trigger items (darkness, smoke) fit disaster-related danger cues; this one points toward a different trauma context and is not coherent with the rest of the selected items.

issues.item: Threat: Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations
issues.explanation: 'Threat from strangers approaching me' implies an interpersonal danger schema. In a natural-disaster case, this is difficult to reconcile with the rest of the profile, which centers on non-interpersonal threat cues (darkness, smoke, physical reactivity, flashback-type reliving). There are no appraisals or memory items supporting a generalized interpersonal threat pattern, so this item is a poor fit with the trauma type and overall formulation.

For a natural-disaster trauma, smoke/fire/flames can be plausible only in certain disaster contexts, but pairing them with darkness as the third trigger makes the trigger set look more like a fire-related trauma profile than a coherent general natural-disaster profile. Darkness is not impossible, but alongside smoke and flames it weakens trauma-type coherence and the trigger pattern is hard to explain without a more specific fire disaster context.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts
issues.explanation: Within maladaptive strategies, self-blame rumination and prevention rumination fit a perseverative threat-focused coping style, but 'I force myself to think only positive thoughts' points toward deliberate suppression/overcontrol in a different direction. It is not impossible, but in this sparse profile it sits awkwardly with the otherwise repetitive self-blaming/what-if style and is less clearly aligned with the strong Triggers ↔ Maladaptive Strategies loop than another avoidance or safety strategy would be.

issues.item: Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
issues.explanation: The profile includes only Triggers, Threat, and Maladaptive Strategies, which is acceptable given the formulation, but within Threat the selected items mix reminder-triggered reactivity with a dissociative re-experiencing item ('flashbacks'). For this trauma type and the rest of the profile, flashbacks are possible but are not well supported by the accompanying Trigger and Strategy items, which emphasize smoke/fire/weather reminders and rumination/suppression rather than dissociative reliving.

issues.item: Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
issues.explanation: The trigger set is coherent for a natural disaster if the event involved wildfire or smoke, but the profile does not otherwise specify a fire-related disaster context. Smoke and fire/flames are narrower and more specific than 'natural disaster' alone, so without matching memory or appraisal content they make the trigger pattern feel overly specific relative to the rest of the report.

issues.item: Threat: Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
issues.explanation: The strongest formulation links are Triggers ↔ Threat and Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies, which are partly reflected by reminder-linked physical reactivity and suppression. However, the maladaptive strategies are dominated by self-blame/prevention rumination, while there are no Negative Appraisal items and no clear cross-node support for guilt/responsibility themes. This makes the rumination content weakly integrated with the rest of the selected items.

vignette:
Rodrigo is a 75-year-old married man of Latin American descent who works as a QA engineer, a role that has anchored his sense of precision and control for decades. He presented for psychological evaluation following a wildfire that swept through his rural community approximately fourteen months ago, during a stretch of dry, windless heat that he now finds almost impossible to describe without his voice faltering. The fire moved faster than anyone had anticipated. Rodrigo was at home when a neighbor's frantic knock brought him to the front door, and what he saw - a wall of orange and black consuming the tree line less than half a mile away - remains, in his words, "burned into the back of my eyes." He had perhaps twenty minutes to gather what he could before the evacuation order came. Several homes on his street were lost. His own survived, but only barely, and the smell of smoke hung in the air for days afterward, seeping through every window seal and settling into furniture, clothing, the walls themselves.

In the weeks that followed, Rodrigo found himself unable to move through ordinary life without the disaster pressing in. The triggers that now hold the most power over him are precisely those that were most present in those twenty minutes: the smell of smoke, the sight of open flame, and weather conditions that resemble that afternoon's dry, still heat. He works from home as a QA engineer, reviewing software systems for failure points - a job that requires sustained concentration - and on days when a neighbor burns yard debris or the summer air sits heavy and motionless, the smell drifts through his window and his focus collapses entirely. His body responds before his mind can intervene: his heart pounds, his chest tightens, his hands begin to shake. These strong physical reactions feel, to Rodrigo, like evidence that something is genuinely wrong, that the threat is real and present, and so his vigilance sharpens further - he finds himself scanning the horizon from his desk window, watching the sky for smoke columns, checking weather forecasts multiple times a day. That state of sustained alertness, in turn, lowers his threshold for surprise; ordinary sounds - a door closing, a car backfiring - send a jolt through him that leaves him embarrassed and exhausted.

What makes the cycle particularly tenacious is the way his heightened threat state feeds back into the very sensory world he is trying to monitor. Because he is already scanning, he notices the faint smell of a distant barbecue, the flicker of a candle across the room, the particular quality of a dry afternoon, in ways he never would have before. These perceptions, once registered, pull him immediately back into the disaster. When that happens, Rodrigo does not simply re-experience the fear - he begins to interrogate himself. He dwells on decisions he made that day: why hadn't he cleared the brush along the fence line that spring, why hadn't he insisted his wife leave earlier, why hadn't he been more prepared. He rehearses alternative timelines in which a different version of himself had acted with the foresight the situation demanded. This rumination, though it feels to him like problem-solving, keeps the emotional intensity of the event alive and close, which means the next encounter with smoke or flame or still heat arrives with the full weight of unresolved distress already loaded. When the rumination becomes unbearable, he tries to push the thoughts away entirely - to concentrate on a work task, to redirect his attention - but the suppression is unreliable, and the thoughts return with renewed force, often accompanied by the physical arousal he was trying to escape, which only confirms to him that he remains in danger.

Over the past year, Rodrigo has become quieter at home. His wife has noticed that he avoids sitting on the back porch in summer, that he leaves rooms where candles are lit, that he is short-tempered in ways that are new to him. He has not told her the full extent of what he experiences, partly because he believes, with quiet conviction, that a man his age should have been able to prevent this - or at least to recover from it by now. What finally brought him to seek help was a review cycle at work in which he missed a significant software defect, something he attributes directly to the days of fragmented concentration that followed a particularly smoky afternoon. For a man whose professional identity rests on catching what others miss, that failure felt intolerable. He arrives at treatment hoping, above all, to be able to work again without the past ambushing him - and afraid, beneath that, that it never will.
